steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting a simple open-loop baseline for RL locomotion tasks. Argue against the growing complexity of deep RL, motivate simpler baselines and prior knowledge, state our goal, and finish with a short contributions subsection.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Progress of DRL vs. growing algorithmic complexity and its problems
2. Simpler baselines and the case for prior knowledge
3. Our open-loop baseline and its purpose
4. Contributions (subsection)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. DRL complexity
- remarkable strides in DRL; robotic control pushed to new frontiers
- dominant trend: steady escalation of algorithmic complexity
- many implementation details needed for satisfactory performance -> reproducibility crisis
- even SOTA struggles on simple problems: Mountain Car, Swimmer

2. Simpler alternatives
- some works went against the trend: simpler baselines, scalable alternatives for RL tasks
- raised questions about evaluation and trends in RL; need for simplicity
- generality of complex RL comes at price of task-design specificity: tedious reward engineering
- we advocate prior knowledge to reduce complexity (algorithm + task formulation) for problem categories like locomotion

3. This paper
- open-loop model-free strategy as baseline for locomotion
- study + compare to DRL in different scenarios; not to replace DRL but highlight limitations, insights, reflection on costs of complexity and generality

## 1.1 Contributions
- open-loop model-free baseline: sparse rewards, high sensory noise, very few parameters (order of tens, Section 2)
- importance of prior knowledge + right policy structure (Section 4.2)
- robustness of RL algorithms to noise and sensor failure (Section 4.3)
- sim-to-real transfer without randomization or reward engineering, where deep RL fails (Section 4.4)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has made remarkable progress in recent years and has pushed robotic control to new frontiers. But a dominant trend in the field is that the algorithms keep getting more complex. As a result, the latest algorithms need lots of implementation details to reach satisfactory performance, and this leads to a worrying reproducibility crisis. Also, even state-of-the-art DRL models struggle with problems that look simple, like the Mountain Car environment or the Swimmer task.

Luckily, some works have gone against this direction and tried to find simpler baselines and scalable alternatives for RL tasks. These efforts raised questions about how RL is evaluated and about the trends in RL, and they also emphasized that the field needs simplicity. The generality of complex RL algorithms also has a cost in terms of specificity in how the task is designed, in the form of tedious reward engineering. We advocate using prior knowledge to reduce complexity, both in the algorithm and in the task formulation, when dealing with specific categories of problems such as locomotion tasks.

3. This paper
- open-loop model-free strategy as baseline for locomotion
- study + compare to DRL in different scenarios; not to replace DRL but highlight limitations, insights, reflection on costs of complexity and generality

## 1.1 Contributions
- open-loop model-free baseline: sparse rewards, high sensory noise, very few parameters (order of tens, Section 2)
- importance of prior knowledge + right policy structure (Section 4.2)
- robustness of RL algorithms to noise and sensor failure (Section 4.3)
- sim-to-real transfer without randomization or reward engineering, where deep RL fails (Section 4.4)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has made remarkable progress in recent years and has pushed robotic control to new frontiers. But a dominant trend in the field is that the algorithms keep getting more complex. As a result, the latest algorithms need lots of implementation details to reach satisfactory performance, and this leads to a worrying reproducibility crisis. Also, even state-of-the-art DRL models struggle with problems that look simple, like the Mountain Car environment or the Swimmer task.

Luckily, some works have gone against this direction and tried to find simpler baselines and scalable alternatives for RL tasks. These efforts raised questions about how RL is evaluated and about the trends in RL, and they also emphasized that the field needs simplicity. The generality of complex RL algorithms also has a cost in terms of specificity in how the task is designed, in the form of tedious reward engineering. We advocate using prior knowledge to reduce complexity, both in the algorithm and in the task formulation, when dealing with specific categories of problems such as locomotion tasks.

In this paper we introduce an open-loop model-free strategy as a baseline for locomotion challenges. We study the baseline and compare it to DRL algorithms in different scenarios. Our goal is not to replace them but to show their current limitations, give insights, and encourage reflection on the costs of complexity and generality.

## 1.1 Contributions

The main contributions of our paper are:

- an open-loop model-free baseline for learning locomotion that can deal with sparse rewards and high sensory noise and needs very few parameters (on the order of tens, Section 2),

- showing that prior knowledge and choosing the right policy structure are important (Section 4.2),

- a study of how robust RL algorithms are to noise and sensor failure (Section 4.3),

- showing successful transfer from simulation to reality without any randomization or reward engineering, in a case where deep RL algorithms fail (Section 4.4).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The field of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has made remarkable strides in recent years, pushing robotic control to new frontiers [1,2]. However, a dominant trend in the field is the steady escalation of algorithmic complexity. As a result, the latest algorithms require many implementation details to achieve satisfactory performance [3], leading to a concerning reproducibility crisis [4]. Moreover, even state-of-the-art DRL models struggle with seemingly simple problems, such as the Mountain Car environment [5] or the Swimmer task [6,7].

Fortunately, several works have gone against this direction and tried to find simpler baselines and scalable alternatives for RL tasks [8,9,10]. These efforts have raised questions about evaluation and trends in RL [11], and have also emphasized the need for simplicity in the field. The generality of complex RL algorithms also comes at the price of specificity in task design, in the form of tedious reward engineering [12]. We advocate leveraging prior knowledge to reduce complexity, both in the algorithm and in the task formulation, when tackling specific problem categories such as locomotion tasks.

In this paper, we introduce an open-loop model-free strategy that serves as a baseline for locomotion challenges. By studying the baseline and comparing it to DRL algorithms in different scenarios, we do not aim to replace them, but to highlight their existing limitations, provide insights, and encourage reflection on the costs of complexity and generality.

## 1.1 Contributions

In summary, the main contributions of our paper are:

- an open-loop model-free baseline for learning locomotion that handles sparse rewards and high sensory noise and requires very few parameters (on the order of tens, Section 2),

- showing the importance of prior knowledge and of choosing the right policy structure (Section 4.2),

- a study of the robustness of RL algorithms to noise and sensor failure (Section 4.3),

- showing successful simulation to reality transfer, without any randomization or reward engineering, where deep RL algorithms fail (Section 4.4).
